kangaroo-at-2017-junior-01.title: Compute
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-01.body:
Numerator $20 \cdot 17 = 340$, denominator $2 + 0 + 1 + 7 = 10$, so the value is $34$.

**Answer: (C) 34**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-02.title: Combine the two moves
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-02.body:
Flipping the glass over its right edge mirrors the word left-to-right: it reads OORAGNAK with mirrored letters (like option D). Turning by $180^\circ$ on the table then turns everything upside down and back to front again. Together the two moves are the same as flipping the glass over its bottom edge: the word reads KANGAROO from left to right, but every letter is upside down (mirrored top-to-bottom). The parallelogram-shaped glass is also mirrored top-to-bottom. This is picture (E).

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-03.title: Subtract the covering stars
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-03.body:
From the outside in, the stars are grey (16), white (9), grey (4), white (1). The visible part of the biggest grey star is $16 - 9 = 7$ cm², the visible part of the small grey star is $4 - 1 = 3$ cm². Total $7 + 3 = 10$ cm².

**Answer: (B) 10 cm²**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-04.title: Share equally
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-04.body:
Together they have $24 + 3 \cdot 12 = 60$ Euros, so each should end with $15$. Each sister needs $3$ more, and Maria gives away $3 \cdot 3 = 9$, keeping $15$.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-04.title: Share Maria's surplus
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-04.body:
Maria has $12$ Euros more than each sister. This surplus must be split among all 4 girls: $12 : 4 = 3$ Euros each, so she gives each sister 3 Euros.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-05.title: Peaks and valleys
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-05.body:
On a straight piece the centre moves parallel to the track at distance $r$.
- At a **peak**, the wheel tips over the corner: the corner stays the contact point, so the centre moves on a circular arc of radius $r$ around it — the path is **rounded** there.
- In a **valley**, the wheel touches both sides at once and passes straight from one parallel line to the next — the path has a **sharp corner** there.

Rounded peaks and pointed valleys: picture (E).

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-06.title: Count both arcs
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-06.body:
Clockwise from Bianca to Antonia there are 4 girls strictly between them (Antonia is number 6). Anticlockwise there are 7 girls between them (Antonia is number 9). Total: Bianca + Antonia + $4 + 7 = 13$.

**Answer: (C) 13**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-06.title: Formula
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-06.body:
Going once around, the two counts together count Bianca and Antonia twice: $n = 6 + 9 - 2 = 13$.

**Answer: (C) 13**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-07.title: Count the turns
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-07.body:
The circumference is $2\pi$, so rolling $11\pi$ means $\frac{11\pi}{2\pi} = 5\frac12$ full turns. Full turns don't change the picture, so the circle ends up turned by half a turn ($180^\circ$) compared with the start: the white part, which was at the top, is now at the bottom, and grey and black swap sides (black on the left, grey on the right). That is picture (E).

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-09.title: Multiply fractions
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-09.body:
Adults are $\frac78$ of the guests; women are $\frac47$ of the adults. So adult women are $\frac78 \cdot \frac47 = \frac48 = \frac12$ of all guests.

**Answer: (A) $\frac12$**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-09.title: Choose a number of guests
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-09.body:
Take 56 guests: 7 are underage, 49 are adults, of whom $21$ are men and $28$ women. $\frac{28}{56} = \frac12$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac12$**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-10.title: Pigeonhole
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-10.body:
With 6 buttons it is possible to have exactly 2 of each colour, so 6 is not enough. With 7 buttons in 3 colours, some colour appears at least $\lceil 7/3 \rceil = 3$ times. So 7 students are needed.

**Answer: (C) 7**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-11.title: Areas with height $h$
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-11.body:
The trapezium has area $\frac{(50 + 20)h}{2} = 35h$. Triangle $AED$ has base $AE$ and the same height $h$, so its area is $\frac{AE \cdot h}{2}$. Half of the trapezium: $\frac{AE \cdot h}{2} = \frac{35h}{2}$, hence $AE = 35$.

**Answer: (C) 35**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-11.title: Compare the two parts
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-11.body:
The other part $EBCD$ is a trapezium with parallel sides $50 - AE$ and $20$. Equal areas with the same height mean $AE = (50 - AE) + 20$, so $2AE = 70$, $AE = 35$.

**Answer: (C) 35**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-12.title: Two windows
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-12.body:
Either $n$ has three digits and $n + 20$ four digits: $n \le 999$ and $n + 20 \ge 1000$, i.e. $980 \le n \le 999$ — 20 numbers. Or $n$ has four digits and $n + 20$ five: $9980 \le n \le 9999$ — another 20 numbers. Total 40.

**Answer: (E) 40**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-13.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-13.body:
Take the triangle $A(0,0)$, $B(2,0)$, $C(1,\sqrt3)$ (area $\sqrt3$) and compute the ratio. The midpoints are $(1,0)$, $(\frac32, \frac{\sqrt3}{2})$, $(\frac12, \frac{\sqrt3}{2})$. The perpendiculars to $AB$ from the two upper midpoints are the vertical lines $x = \frac12$ and $x = \frac32$. The perpendicular from $(1,0)$ to $AC$ has direction $(-\sqrt3, 1)$ and meets $x = \frac12$ at height $\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}$. By symmetry the hexagon has vertices
$$(1,0),\ \left(\tfrac32, \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3}\right),\ \left(\tfrac32, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),\ \left(1, \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\right),\ \left(\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),\ \left(\tfrac12, \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3}\right).$$
All its sides have length $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and it is symmetric under $120^\circ$ turns, so it is a regular hexagon with area $6 \cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot\frac13 = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ — exactly half of $\sqrt3$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac12$**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-14.title: Use the middle number
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-14.body:
With middle number $m$: $(m-1)^2 + m^2 + (m+1)^2 = 3m^2 + 2 = 770$, so $m^2 = 256$, $m = 16$. The biggest number is 17.

Check: $225 + 256 + 289 = 770$.

**Answer: (C) 17**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-15.title: Equal belt length
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-15.body:
Without sliding, the belt moves the same length on both wheels: (number of turns) × (circumference) is the same.
- $B$ and $C$: $6 \cdot c_B = 7 \cdot 30$, so $c_B = 35$ cm.
- $A$ and $B$: $5 \cdot c_A = 4 \cdot c_B = 140$, so $c_A = 28$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 28 cm**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-16.title: Circular arrangement
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-16.body:
The week repeats, so Sunday and Monday are also consecutive: we choose 3 of the 7 days on a circle with no two of them neighbours. Listing them: Mon-Wed-Fri, Mon-Wed-Sat, Mon-Thu-Sat, Tue-Thu-Sat, Tue-Thu-Sun, Tue-Fri-Sun, Wed-Fri-Sun. That's 7.

**Answer: (B) 7**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-16.title: Count via a fixed day
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-16.body:
Plans containing Monday: then Sunday and Tuesday are out, and we pick 2 non-adjacent days from Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat: (Wed, Fri), (Wed, Sat), (Thu, Sat) — 3 plans. Plans without Monday: choose 3 non-adjacent days from the line Tue–Sun (6 days): $\binom{6-3+1}{3} = \binom43 = 4$. Total $3 + 4 = 7$.

**Answer: (B) 7**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-17.title: One unknown difference
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-17.body:
Let the common difference be $d$. Then Viktor $= 184 + d$, Tobias $= 184$, Peter $= 184 - d$, Oskar $= 184 - 2d$. The sum is $736 - 2d = 4 \cdot 178 = 712$, so $d = 12$ and Oskar is $184 - 24 = 160$ cm.

**Answer: (A) 160 cm**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-18.title: Three kinds of days
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-18.body:
Let $m$ = days with rain in the morning only, $a$ = afternoon only, $z$ = dry days. Then $m + a = 7$, $a + z = 5$ (no morning rain), $m + z = 6$ (no afternoon rain). Adding: $2(m + a + z) = 18$, so the holiday lasted $9$ days ($m = 4$, $a = 3$, $z = 2$).

**Answer: (C) 9**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-19.title: Compare overlapping squares
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-19.body:
Label the table
$$\begin{array}{ccc} 3 & b & 1\\ d & e & f\\ 2 & h & x \end{array}$$
Top-left square = bottom-left square: $3 + b + d + e = d + e + 2 + h$, so $b - h = -1$.
Top-right square = bottom-right square: $b + 1 + e + f = e + f + h + x$, so $b - h = x - 1$.

Hence $x - 1 = -1$, i.e. $x = 0$. Such a filling exists, e.g. rows $3, 0, 1$ / $0, 0, 2$ / $2, 1, 0$, where every $2\times2$ square has sum 3.

**Answer: (D) 0**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-20.title: Parity, then size
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-20.body:
Neighbours differ by 1, so the parities alternate: $a, c, e, g$ have one parity and $b, d, f$ the other. If $a, c, e, g$ were odd, the sum would be 4 odd + 3 even = even, but 2017 is odd. So $a, c, e, g$ are even and $b, d, f$ odd — 286 can only be $a, c, e$ or $g$.

If $c = 286$, every other number is at most its distance from $c$ larger: $a, e \le 288$, $b, d \le 287$, $f \le 289$, $g \le 290$, so the sum is at most $288 + 287 + 286 + 287 + 288 + 289 + 290 = 2015 < 2017$. So $c \ne 286$, and by symmetry $e \ne 286$.

$a = 286$ works: $286, 287, 288, 289, 290, 289, 288$ has sum $2017$. By symmetry $g = 286$ works too.

**Answer: (A) only $a$ or $g$**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-21.title: Factorise 882
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-21.body:
$882 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 7^2$. The two factors 7 must go to two different gorillas (49 is too old), and the ages below 18 divisible by 7 are 7 and 14. So two gorillas are 7 and 14 (using the factor 2), and the remaining two ages multiply to $882 : 98 = 9$ and are different: $1$ and $9$.

Ages $1, 7, 9, 14$, sum $31$.

**Answer: (D) 31**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-22.title: One negative, one positive
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-22.body:
The product is negative exactly when one number is negative (3 faces) and the other positive (2 faces). Number of outcomes: $3 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 = 12$ out of $36$, i.e. $\frac{12}{36} = \frac13$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac13$**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-23.title: Pythagoras four times
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-23.body:
Let the diagonals meet at $S$ and set $SA = a$, $SB = b$, $SC = c$, $SD = d$. The four triangles at $S$ are right-angled, so
$$AB^2 + CD^2 = (a^2 + b^2) + (c^2 + d^2) = (b^2 + c^2) + (a^2 + d^2) = BC^2 + AD^2.$$
Thus $AD^2 = 2017^2 + 2019^2 - 2018^2 = (2018 - 1)^2 + (2018 + 1)^2 - 2018^2 = 2018^2 + 2$.

**Answer: (D) $\sqrt{2018^2 + 2}$**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-24.title: Factor out 10101
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-24.body:
$\overline{ababab} = \overline{ab}\cdot 10000 + \overline{ab}\cdot 100 + \overline{ab} = \overline{ab} \cdot 10101$, and $10101 = 3 \cdot 7 \cdot 13 \cdot 37$. So the number is always divisible by 7. The others fail, e.g. $131313$ is odd, not divisible by 5, has digit sum 12 (not divisible by 9), and its alternating digit sum $3-1+3-1+3-1 = 6$ shows it isn't divisible by 11.

**Answer: (C) 7**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-25.title: Sets of digits with sum 7
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-25.body:
The digits used must be different and add up to 7 (digit $k$ fills $k$ places). Each set gives one block per digit, and the blocks can be ordered in any way:
- $\{7\}$: 1 password
- $\{1, 6\}$, $\{2, 5\}$, $\{3, 4\}$: 2 orders each, 6 passwords
- $\{1, 2, 4\}$: $3! = 6$ orders

(0 cannot be used, since it would have to appear 0 times.) Total $1 + 6 + 6 = 13$.

**Answer: (E) 13**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-26.title: Parity triples
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-26.body:
Number the rows 1 (top) to 6 (bottom). Since each tile is the sum of the two tiles below it, any tile together with the two tiles below it has an **even** sum, so among these three at most 2 are odd.

The same holds for a tile and the two tiles two rows further down at the ends of its little pyramid: if $x, y, z$ are adjacent in a row, the tile two rows above is $(x + y) + (y + z) = x + z + 2y$, which has the same parity as $x + z$.

The 21 tiles can be split into 7 such groups of three: the top tile with the two tiles of row 2; the left and right tiles of row 3 each with the two tiles below them in row 4; the middle tile of row 3 with the 2nd and 4th tiles of row 5; and the 1st, 3rd and 5th tiles of row 5 each with the two tiles below them in row 6. Each group has at most 2 odd tiles, so at most $7 \cdot 2 = 14$ odd numbers.

14 is achievable, e.g. with the bottom row $1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2$:
$$\begin{array}{c} 43 \\ 22\quad 21 \\ 11\quad 11\quad 10 \\ 5\quad 6\quad 5\quad 5 \\ 2\quad 3\quad 3\quad 2\quad 3 \\ 1\quad 1\quad 2\quad 1\quad 1\quad 2 \end{array}$$
The odd numbers are $1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 14$.

**Answer: (B) 14**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-27.title: Angle sum of an $n$-gon
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-27.body:
The full sum is $(n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ$, and the missing angle is between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ (the polygon is convex, its vertices lie on a circle). The smallest multiple of $180$ above $2017$ is $12 \cdot 180 = 2160$, so the missing angle is $2160^\circ - 2017^\circ = 143^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $143^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-28.title: Facing pairs and back-to-back pairs
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-28.body:
After the first turn every dancer looks along the circle, either clockwise (C) or anticlockwise (A). Two neighbours face each other when we read "C then A" going clockwise, and they stand back to back when we read "A then C". Going once around the circle, the direction changes from C to A exactly as often as from A to C. So there are as many back-to-back pairs as facing pairs: 10 head-shakers means 5 facing pairs and hence 5 back-to-back pairs.

Turning around swaps C and A for everyone, so the back-to-back pairs become facing pairs and vice versa: again 5 pairs, i.e. 10 dancers.

**Answer: (A) 10**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-29.title: Count the heavier triples
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-29.body:
The total is $621$ g, so the right side is heavier exactly when its three weights have a sum of at least $311$. There are $\binom63 = 20$ ways to choose the right side; since the total is odd there are no ties, and by symmetry (swap the sides) exactly 10 of them have the right side heavier.

Heavy triples **without** 106: from $101, \ldots, 105$ the sum must be $\ge 311$: only $103 + 104 + 105 = 312$ and $102 + 104 + 105 = 311$. So 2 of the 10 distributions don't have 106 on the right, and 8 do: $\frac{8}{10} = 80\%$.

**Answer: (B) 80 %**

kangaroo-at-2017-junior-30.title: Tangent and Pythagoras
kangaroo-at-2017-junior-30.body:
Let $PA = a$ and $MB = r$. As in the diagram, $A$ lies between $P$ and $M$, so $PM = a + r$. The radius $MB$ is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$(a + 6)^2 = PB^2 = PM^2 - r^2 = (a + r)^2 - r^2 = a^2 + 2ar.$$
This gives $12a + 36 = 2ar$, i.e. $r = 6 + \frac{18}{a}$. So $a$ must divide 18: $a \in \{1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18\}$, giving $r \in \{24, 15, 12, 9, 8, 7\}$ — 6 values.

(If $A$ were the far intersection point, then $PB < PA$, impossible.)

**Answer: (D) 6**
